# GT Round E1 — results report

*Prompt GT-P004, deliverables 4 and 6. Written to be read without the programme's internal vocabulary. Numbers are exact-kernel values from `reports/round-e1-tables.json` (result commit `730ef32`, payload `f1727f9d3c3f…`). The behaviour atlas `reports/gt-e1-atlas.md` lists every cell and every channel; this report is a reading of it, not a selection from it.*

Layers are marked: **[O]** model observation, **[M]** mathematical mechanism, **[RS]** Relational Substrate interpretation, **[P]** physical comparison, **[T]** theological premise. No [P] claim is made anywhere in this report.

## 1. What was run, and why

**The model.** A few entities (5, 6 or 7). Between every two of them a relation is present or absent. Relations form and dissolve one at a time. A rule makes some changes more or less likely, multiplying a factor once for every qualifying "witness" nearby. In the HELD set-up three entities form a permanently linked source triangle; the others ("probes") may attach to it or not. The stationary law of every cell is computed exactly, in two clocks:
- **per unit time** (continuous clock): where the system spends its time;
- **per event** (jump clock): what the sequence of changes looks like.

**Why E1.** E0 found that rules which look two steps away (path rules) create a lasting direction of flow — a **handover** cycle: probe–probe relation forms, attachment to the source forms, probe–probe relation dissolves, attachment dissolves. One combined rule, **CSPH**, also gave a small advantage to attachment over the no-rule baseline, shrinking from N=5 to N=6. GT-P003 then found that the advantage depends on the clock and on crowding, and that the same nominal rule might get effectively stronger as N grows (more possible witnesses). E1 asks two questions at once:

1. **Tranche I (8 cells).** The same eight E0B rules, same grades (W4 alphabet), at N=7.
2. **Tranche II (24 cells).** The six non-gradient rules made uniformly stronger (W3: every log-factor × 1.585; W16: × 2) at N=5 and N=6. This shows what "a stronger rule at the same size" does, to compare with what "a bigger system" does.

Plus 16 re-derivations of the published N=5, 6 W4 cells with the same code, so every comparison uses one implementation. These are not new observations.

The plan was frozen and pushed (`4ba2839`) before any round cell ran. All 48 items completed in 24 minutes on four workers (longest cell 615 s, peak 603 MB). No cell was unresolved; every cell passed every numerical check (two-start and third-start agreement, per-entry residual in extended precision, the dense GTH referee at N≤6, the rule strings re-evaluated exactly on sampled states). All identities and controls held: NULL uniform and reversible (Z1), the gradient control on its predicted law (Z2), non-gradient rates in every non-gradient cell (Z3), every published N=5, 6 cell reproduced on the declared robust channels (Z4), and both reversible controls without hub-frame circulation (Z6).

## 2. What changed from N=6 to N=7 at fixed grades

### 2.1 CSPH's attachment advantage is gone at N=7 [O]

| CSPH margin over the null | N=5 | N=6 | N=7 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| raw, per unit time | +0.046 | +0.009 | **−0.067** |
| raw, per event | +0.073 | +0.065 | **+0.002** |
| ceiling-normalised, per unit time | +0.325 | +0.035 | −0.200 |
| ceiling-normalised, per event | +0.511 | +0.260 | +0.005 |
| crowding-adjusted (standardised), per unit time | +0.023 | −0.073 | −0.112 |
| crowding-adjusted, per event | +0.038 | −0.034 | −0.095 |

In every form the N=7 value is at or below the null; the per-event raw margin is +0.002, which is the null to within the size of the effects in this round. **The basin-with-arrow coexistence that E0B found in CSPH (GT-F26) does not survive to N=7 in this model.** This is a finding for this family, this size and these definitions; it is not by itself evidence of an intrinsic finite-size effect, of witness amplification, or of a failure of the wider picture (plan, stop-rule reading).

### 2.2 Why the advantage disappeared: a sparse-only preference, less time sparse [O, M]

The advantage is an average over how many free relations are present (k). Resolved by k (frozen channel: the a/k profile):

| CSPH, per unit time | attachment per free relation at k = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 | null | time spent at k ≤ 2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| N=5 | 0.855, 0.924, 0.922, 0.870, 0.850 | 0.857 | 0.86 |
| N=6 | 0.771, 0.792, 0.746, 0.701, 0.667 | 0.750 | 0.68 |
| N=7 | 0.718, 0.701, 0.625, 0.533, 0.472 | 0.667 | 0.42 |

At N=7 the preference for attachment is still there when only one or two relations are free (excess +0.03 to +0.05 over the null, against +0.02 to +0.04 at N=6). At three to five free relations the rule prefers probe–probe relations, more strongly than at N=6 (k=4: −0.13 against −0.05). And the system spends less of its time in the sparse regime: with more probes there are more ways to have several free relations. The same pattern holds per event (excess at k ≤ 3; time at k ≤ 2 falls 0.62 → 0.43 → 0.24).

A **post hoc** decomposition (computed after the results; not a frozen comparison; `reports/e1-margin-composition-posthoc.json`) writes the margin as the occupancy-weighted average of the per-density excess and splits its change into an occupancy part and a preference part. For CSPH from N=6 to N=7: per unit time −0.075 = −0.025 (occupancy) − 0.050 (preference); per event −0.063 = −0.027 − 0.036. **About a third of the loss is the move to higher density; two thirds is a stronger anti-attachment preference at moderate density.** The local preference at very low density survives but no longer dominates.

### 2.3 The handover persists, unchanged in orientation [O]

All four steps of the handover cycle run in the E0 direction **in all 30 non-gradient cells** (six families × every size and alphabet), and in none of the reversible controls. The handover index (forward-minus-reverse probability over the four steps, per event pair) at N = 5, 6, 7:

| | CSPH | CSPF | CWPH | CWPF | PATHF | PATHH |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| index | 0.036, 0.043, 0.042 | 0.070, 0.062, 0.040 | 0.049, 0.052, 0.047 | 0.087, 0.071, 0.047 | 0.095, 0.076, 0.050 | 0.055, 0.056, 0.049 |
| irreversible flux | 0.090, 0.136, 0.157 | 0.126, 0.162, 0.147 | 0.098, 0.136, 0.150 | 0.134, 0.161, 0.154 | 0.132, 0.158, 0.153 | 0.088, 0.124, 0.140 |

For rules that act on dissolution (…H) the handover's per-event weight is roughly constant with N; for rules that act on formation (…F) it shrinks. Total irreversible flux is roughly constant from N=6 to N=7 (0.14–0.16 in all six). **The arrow does not weaken with size in total; the attachment advantage does. Arrow and basin separate further at N=7.** [O]

### 2.4 Other changes with N [O]

- **Detachment stays high.** In every non-gradient cell a probe is detached about 55–58% of the time at N=7 (NULL: 1.8%; gradient control: 0.004%). At N=7, three or four of the four probes are often detached at once (CSPH: 49% of the time per unit time). The repulsive character of every arrow-carrying rule (GT-F18) persists.
- **The equal-ratio gap keeps growing, more slowly.** Pairs with the same local ratios but acting on formation versus dissolution differ in stationary law by L1 0.18–0.22 (N=5), 0.32–0.49 (N=6), 0.37–0.62 (N=7). Growth slows from ×1.8–2.3 to ×1.15–1.25.
- **Near/far activity contrast weakens in the arrow cells.** The ratio of probe activity near the source to activity farther out (ρ) falls toward 1 in formation-acting rules (CSPF 1.18 → 1.09, PATHF 1.11 → 1.03 per unit time). In the gradient control it falls below 1 and keeps falling (CLOSEW 1.03 → 0.89 → 0.61): near-source slowing grows with N there, consistent with G1's kinetic account.
- **Attachments last longer, measured in events.** The correlation time of "probe attached" grows with N in every non-gradient family (e.g. CSPH 4.6 → 5.9 → 7.0 mean events; CWPH 2.4 → 3.5 → 4.6; PATHF 1.7 → 3.1 → 4.8).
- **Hubs.** The share of time a probe alone is the best-connected entity rises with N in every family (N=7: 0.03–0.10), tracking the NULL rate (0.016 → 0.055 → 0.108) but staying below it. This is the changing geometry of the HELD set-up (more probes, smaller source share 3/N), not an emergent centre.
- **The gradient control (CLOSEW) fills up.** Free-relation density 0.81 → 0.90 → 0.96. Its raw margin falls to about zero (+0.0008) because it is near the ceiling, while its crowding-adjusted margin grows (+0.022 → +0.034 → +0.042). The only rule in the round with a crowding-adjusted attachment preference that grows with N is the reversible gradient control, not any arrow-carrying rule.

## 3. Size versus strength

### 3.1 How much stronger do the rules actually act at N=7? [O]

A path rule can see up to 12, 24 and 40 witnesses at N = 5, 6, 7. But the witnesses a rule *actually uses* at the events that happen grew very little. The ratio of mean engaged log-weight N=7 / N=6, per component:

| | closure part | path part |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CSPH | 0.87 | 1.05 |
| CSPF | 0.99 | 0.87 |
| CWPH | 0.87 | 1.06 |
| CWPF | 1.05 | 0.92 |
| PATHF | — | 0.94 |
| PATHH | — | 1.08 |
| CLOSEW (gradient) | 1.35 | — |

Every non-gradient component is between 0.87 and 1.08, far below the strengthening bracket (1.585 for W3, 2 for W16). The arrow-carrying rules steer the system into states with few witnesses, so their effective strength barely changes with size. **Witness amplification, as actually engaged, is small from N=6 to N=7.** (The gradient control does amplify, 1.35, because it fills the graph.)

### 3.2 Does "stronger at N=5" reproduce the known step N=5 → N=6? [O]

The frozen calibration compares, channel by channel (17 declared channels), the step N=5 W4 → N=5 W16 (log-strength doubled, matching the witness maximum 12 → 24) with the published step N=5 → N=6 at W4.

| Family | verdict (frozen rule) | channels with the same direction | of which comparable in size |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PATHF (clean case) | direction only | 12 of 17 | 3 |
| PATHH (clean case) | direction only | 14 of 16 | 5 |
| CWPF | direction only | 13 of 17 | 4 |
| CWPH | direction only | 15 of 17 | 6 |
| CSPF | direction only | 15 of 17 | 6 |
| CSPH | **poor proxy** | 10 of 17 | 0 |

Strengthening moves most channels in the same direction as growing the system, but by a different amount, and in no family does it reproduce the step in size. For CSPH it is a poor proxy: it gets 7 channels in the wrong direction, including the per-event margin, irreversible flux and the handover index. Under the frozen reading rule, CSPH's N=7 comparison below is reported but not used as evidence for or against amplification.

### 3.3 Is the N=6 → N=7 step what strengthening does at N=6? [O]

Per channel, the N=6 → N=7 step is compared with the W3 and W16 responses at N=6. Pooled over the six families (102 channel readings): 16 in the direction and size range of strengthening, 55 in the direction but outside the range, 22 opposite, 8 with a non-monotone strength response, 1 negligible. Almost all "outside the range" readings are **smaller** than strengthening would produce, which is what the engaged-load ratio of about 1 predicts.

Channels that run **opposite** to strengthening in most families:
- **probe-only hub share** (all six families): N raises it, strengthening lowers it — a geometric effect of adding probes;
- **near/far activity ratio** (five families);
- in CSPH, the **per-event margin and irreversible flux**: strengthening raises both, size lowers the margin and raises the flux less;
- the **handover index** in CWPH and PATHH: strengthening raises it, size leaves it flat or slightly lower.

Detachment is the clearest contrast: strengthening at N=6 drives probe detachment from 0.52–0.55 to 0.84–0.89; going to N=7 changes it only to 0.55–0.58.

### 3.4 Size and strength act on the margin differently [O, M]

The same post hoc decomposition (labelled as such) applied to the strengthening step separates the two operations:

| Margin change, per unit time | total | occupancy part | preference part |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CSPH, size N=6 → 7 | −0.075 | −0.025 | −0.050 |
| CSPH, strength N=6 W4 → W16 | −0.306 | +0.007 | −0.312 |
| CWPH, size | −0.065 | −0.031 | −0.035 |
| CWPH, strength | −0.318 | +0.018 | −0.336 |
| PATHH, size | −0.055 | −0.032 | −0.023 |
| PATHH, strength | −0.268 | +0.029 | −0.296 |

- **Strength acts almost entirely through the per-density preference**, and its occupancy part has the opposite sign: strengthening crowds the system into low density (CSPH time at k ≤ 2: 0.68 → 0.83), which by itself would *raise* the margin. In CSPH it also **splits the clocks**: per event the preference survives (attachment per free relation at k = 1–3: 0.87, 0.91, 0.85 against the null 0.75) and the per-event margin rises (+0.065 → +0.092), while per unit time it collapses (0.58, 0.65, 0.22) and the margin falls (+0.009 → −0.297). In CWPH and PATHH strengthening lowers the preference in both clocks.
- **Size acts through both parts**, and its occupancy part is negative in all three dissolution-acting families and both clocks (−0.024 to −0.032): growing the system moves occupancy toward higher density, the opposite of what strengthening does.
- In the formation-acting families (CSPF, CWPF, PATHF) the occupancy part is small for both operations (|·| ≤ 0.02) and both act through the preference.

So "the rule got stronger" and "the system got bigger" are distinguishable in this grammar: they move occupancy in opposite directions, and strengthening changes the preference several times more than one step of size. [M: the margin is exactly Σ_k q(k)·x(k), an average of the per-density excess x over the attachment-weighted density profile q; the split depends on the order of the two terms, and the reported split uses the smaller system's preference and the larger system's profile.]

### 3.5 What remains confounded

- **Intrinsic size dependence.** With three sizes, what remains after the measured effects (engaged load, density composition, ceiling) has no unique interpretation.
- **Composite balance.** Uniform strengthening scales closure and path parts together. In CSPH the engaged closure load fell (0.87) while the path load rose (1.05) from N=6 to N=7; the bracket cannot reproduce that rebalancing.
- **Source share.** The fixed source triangle is 60%, 50%, 43% of the entities at N = 5, 6, 7, and the null ceiling falls with it. Neither is separable from N in HELD.
- **Counterfactual standardisation.** The crowding-adjusted margin reweights to the NULL density profile, which at N=7 puts most weight on k = 7–11, where CSPH's own mass is 3e-4 to 1e-15 (some flagged rare). It is reported beside the raw margin and never alone. Every rare conditional (mass < 1e-12) is flagged in the tables and not interpreted.
- **Spectrum.** The relaxation spectrum is unavailable in every E1 cell (not computed by the scalable observables); it is not zero.

## 4. Model result versus physical implication

Everything above is **[O]** or **[M]**: properties of a declared stochastic grammar on 5–7 entities. Nothing here is a statement about gravity, time dilation or any physical system **[P]**. In particular:
- the disappearance of CSPH's attachment advantage is not evidence against relational accounts of gravity, and its persistence would not have been evidence for them;
- the handover is an order of events in a toy chain, not a physical arrow of time;
- the near-source slowing in the gradient control is a kinetic property of that rule (G1), not a clock-rate effect.

The **[RS]** reading, kept separate: the round sharpens a distinction the RS framework can use — between *succession* (a stationary order of actualisation, here robust to size and strength) and *gathering* (a time-weighted preference for relation to a reference, here fragile, density-dependent and clock-dependent). In this grammar the two are produced by the same rules but are not coupled; the RS layer should not treat one as evidence of the other. No theological premise **[T]** is tested or used.

- FREE N=7 (option D) was not authorised; whether a centre emerges without a fixed source at N=7 remains open.
- No grade, alphabet or size was added after freezing; no cell was re-run.
- Trajectories (four per cell, 400 events) were generated and are replayable from their seeds, but add no independent insight beyond the exact laws; the atlas does not reproduce them.

# GT-E2 controlled dissolution analysis

*Prompt GT-P005, deliverable 7. From the frozen E2A and E2B tables (`reports/round-e2a-tables.json`, result `32ac7f6`; `reports/round-e2b-tables.json`, result `ecb3e73`). All quantities are exact-kernel values. "Removing g" is an experimental instrument: a stationary state with relation g present is compared with the same state without g. It is not a claim that the model contains interventions.*

## 1. What was compared

For a relation g that is present in a state x, the matched partner x⁻ is x with g removed. Both x and x⁻ are in the recurrent class, and the rule set is the same for both. x is drawn from the stationary per-event law, restricted to states containing g.

For every other relation slot f, and the action available on it (form or dissolve), the analysis records five quantities:

| Mechanism (GT-P005 section 4) | Quantity |
| --- | --- |
| Strict support enabling / disabling | Share of matched pairs where f's rate is 0 at x and positive at x⁻ (enabling), or the reverse (disabling) |
| Rate enabling / suppression | Mean of log W(x⁻, f) / W(x, f), where both are positive |
| Opportunity (denominator) effect | Mean of log P(x⁻, f) / P(x, f) minus the rate log ratio. This is the part of the next-event change due only to the total rate of competing events |
| Indirect pathway effect | Change in the probability that f happens within H = 1, 2, 4, 8 events. E2B adds the race probability that f happens before g is restored |
| Temporal precedence | p(next event is f, given that g was just dissolved) ÷ p(an event is f): the observed sequence, without intervention |

## 2. Soft rules: no strict enabling; most of the effect is opportunity

There are 288 groups across the soft cells: support class × target class × action, over all soft E2A cells. They show:
- **No strict enabling or disabling.** This follows from the definitions: a positive soft factor never makes a positive rate zero.
- **In 170 groups (59%), the opportunity part is larger than the rate part.** Removing g changes which event comes next mainly by changing how fast everything else happens.
- **In 54 groups (19%), the next-event probability moves opposite to f's own rate.** f becomes more likely next although its own rate fell, or the reverse. This is a pure denominator effect.

**The handover's release step** (the probe–probe relation P is removed; the target is the attachment A sharing that probe), in the unsaturated σ > 0 cells at HELD N=5:

| Cell | Rate log ratio | Opportunity part | Next-event log ratio | Δ passage, 1 event | Δ passage, 8 events | Precedence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PATHH weak_favour | −0.169 | +0.563 | +0.394 | +0.112 | +0.011 | 1.14 |
| PATHH strong_favour | −0.125 | +0.763 | +0.638 | +0.288 | +0.001 | 1.40 |
| PATHF weak_suppress | 0 | +0.288 | +0.288 | +0.118 | +0.003 | 0.85 |
| PATHF strong_suppress | 0 | +0.556 | +0.556 | +0.348 | 0.000 | 0.69 |
| PFD weak_suppress+weak_favour | −0.018 | +0.594 | +0.576 | +0.326 | +0.000 | 1.07 |

In every one of these cells, dissolving P makes the attachment's dissolution more likely *as the next event*. But the attachment's own dissolution rate is unchanged (path-form rules) or **lower** (path-dissolve rules). The increase comes entirely from the opportunity term: P's own fast dissolution is gone from the competition. The effect on whether A dissolves within 8 events is negligible (≤ 0.011). Observed precedence is near 1 and can fall below it.

**Reading.** In soft rules the handover is a **kinetic sequence**, ordered by competition for the next event. It is not transition-enabling dissolution in any stronger sense. This is the negative finding GT-P005 allowed for.

## 3. Hard components: strict enabling, with three different relations to direction

| Cell (N=5) | Strict enabling (largest group share) | Irreversible flux | Direction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hard closure exclusion alone (EXCL), HELD / FREE | 0.87 / 0.27 (A→A same probe, formation; FREE: adjacent formation) | 1e-15 | **None** (reversible) |
| Hard adjacency exclusion alone, FREE | 0.60 | 8e-16 | **None** (reversible) |
| Hard adjacency exclusion + any path term, FREE | 0.60 | 8e-16 | **None.** The path terms are inert (formal note 5.3) |
| Hard closure exclusion + path term, σ > 0 (EXPH, EXPF), HELD | 0.96, 0.98 | 0.076, 0.126 | Soft circulation following σ (+) |
| Hard closure exclusion + path term, σ < 0, HELD | 0.76, 0.72 | 0.049, 0.016 | Soft circulation following σ (−); visible because the exclusion keeps density low |
| Hard path-form exclusion (± path_dissolve), FREE | 0.47 (disjoint), 0.19 (adjacent) | 0.17–0.26 | **One-way release**; orientation + whatever the soft σ (formal note 5.5) |
| Hard path-form or adjacency exclusion, HELD | 0 (the held source is a witness; formal note 5.4) | 0 | Degenerate two-state chain |

**Strict enabling is neither necessary nor sufficient for directed succession in this grammar.**
- **Not necessary:** every soft cell with σ ≠ 0 circulates without any strict enabling.
- **Not sufficient:** EXCL and the hard adjacency exclusions enable strictly and are reversible.

## 4. Does an enabled event actually follow?

E2B's race probability asks whether, from x⁻, the target f happens before g is restored.

| Cell (FREE N=5 unless noted) | Group | f wins, enabled instances | f wins, all instances from x⁻ | f wins, from x with g present |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hard path-form + path_dissolve weak_favour | disjoint formation | 0.514 | 0.463 | 0.142 |
| Hard path-form + path_dissolve weak_favour | adjacent formation | 0.495 | 0.465 | 0.232 |
| Hard closure + path_dissolve weak_suppress | adjacent formation | 0.491 | 0.386 | 0.279 |
| Hard closure + path_dissolve weak_suppress, HELD | attachment → attachment, same probe | 0.491 | 0.430 | 0.000 |
| Hard adjacency exclusion alone | adjacent formation | 0.500 | 0.443 | 0.000 |

- **Removing the support opens a window.** An enabled event wins the race against restoration about half the time (0.49–0.53). With the support present, the same event wins 0.00–0.28 of the time.
- **It is not a commitment.** Restoring the support competes about evenly with the enabled event.
- **Observed precedence misses this.** In the one-way cell, the strictly enabled formations are *less* likely than average as the next event after an executed dissolution (precedence 0.72 adjacent, 0.95 disjoint). The counterfactual question (what removal makes possible) and the observational one (what tends to follow) separate.

## 5. Where "transition-enabling dissolution" exists, in this grammar

| Sense | Exists? | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Temporal precedence (A dissolved, then B happened) | Yes, in every irreversible cell | Event-order statistics |
| Rate enabling | Yes, soft and hard | Matched rate log ratios; often outweighed by opportunity |
| Opportunity (denominator) effect | Yes; dominant in 59% of soft groups | Matched jump-ratio decomposition |
| Indirect pathway (passage within H events, race) | Yes. In soft rules it is small for the handover release step (≤ 0.011 at 8 events) and up to 0.12 in other groups. In hard rules it is large (race about 0.5 against ≤ 0.28) | Passage and race channels |
| Strict support enabling | Only with a hard component | EXCL, EXPH, EXPF, hard adjacency and path-form exclusions |
| Strict enabling **with** direction | With a hard component plus soft circulation, or with one-way release | EXPH/EXPF; hard path-form exclusion |
| Irreversible release (a released relation cannot return while supported) | Only under hard path-form exclusion | 100% of one-way flux is release |

For CL-Q05 ("when does controlled dissolution enable a distinct configuration rather than merely remove one?"):
- In this grammar, dissolution enables a distinct configuration *strictly* only through hard formation exclusions. It does so whether or not the dynamics has a direction.
- The soft handover enables only in the opportunity sense.

This is a GT model result. It is offered to the laboratory as a suggested finding, not entered in its records (`reports/gt-e2-synthesis.md`, section 6).

## 5. HELD and FREE framing

- **HELD imposes the reference.** The orientation is source-relative because source vertices carry two extra neighbours (formal note, corollary 3). Under hard path-form or adjacency exclusion, the source triangle is itself a witness and blocks every attachment (formal note 5.4).
- **FREE has no reference.** Orientation is still legible, relative to an *induced* one: the better-connected partner. The partner frame is defined in every state from current degrees, without a held structure or a hub label.
- **Neither frame is evidence of an emergent centre.** The partner frame refers to local degree differences, not to a persistent hub.

## 6. Counterexamples and boundaries found

1. **σ does not set the orientation when one-way transitions are present.** Hard path-form plus path_dissolve weak_suppress: σ < 0, partner index +0.070.
2. **Local affinity does not fix local current.** Up to 36% of circulation runs counter to its square's affinity.
3. **Strict enabling is neither necessary nor sufficient for direction** (EXCL, hard adjacency exclusion; soft σ ≠ 0 cells).
4. **One-step precedence is not counterfactual enabling** (one-way cell).
5. **The handover's release step is an opportunity effect in soft rules** (own rate unchanged or lower).
6. **Hard adjacency exclusion removes the incidence on which every path term acts.**
7. **The held source blocks attachment under hard path-form or adjacency exclusion.**

# What the handover is, and when dissolving a relation enables anything

*A plain-English report for the human researcher on prompt GT-P005 (two rounds, E2A and E2B, 14 October 2026). It assumes no knowledge of the code. Detailed documents are listed at the end.*

## The question you asked

In the earlier experiments, a repeated pattern of four changes kept appearing. We called it the **handover**:
1. a relation forms between two outer entities;
2. one of them links to the fixed source;
3. the relation between the outer entities dissolves;
4. the link to the source dissolves.

It ran in the same direction in all 30 cases tested in E1. You asked:
- what produces this kind of ordered sequence;
- whether it is general or depends on choices we made;
- whether "a relation dissolving" actually *enables* the next change, or only comes before it.

## What I did

I worked in the smallest systems that can show the pattern: five entities, plus a small check at six. I used only rules the framework already has, so no new kind of rule was introduced.

**Before running anything**, I worked through the rules on paper. That gave an exact formula for how strongly each small loop of four changes is pushed one way rather than the other. I checked it on made-up rule strengths that the experiments never use.

**Round E2A** (46 cases, frozen before running):
- every strength of the two path rules (the rules that look two steps away);
- the four ways to combine them;
- controls that should show no direction at all;
- cases with "hard" rules that forbid some changes outright;
- two cases built to lower crowding;

each with and without a fixed source.

**Round E2B** (18 cases, chosen *because* of what E2A showed, and frozen before running) looked at the three kinds of hard rule combined with path rules of both directions.

All 64 cases finished. Every built-in check passed.

## What I found

**1. The direction of the handover is explained exactly, and it is not universal.**
- The formula says something simple. When two relations share an entity, the rules favour keeping the one whose *other* end is better connected and letting go of the one whose other end is less connected.
- With a fixed source, the source's members always have two extra links. So "keep the link to the source, let the outer relation go" is the favoured direction. That is the handover.
- Whether it runs forward or backward depends on a single number I'll call **σ**: whether the path rules mainly speed up dissolving or mainly slow down forming.
- Every rule in the earlier rounds had σ positive, which is why the direction never changed. It was a consequence of the rules we happened to choose, not a law of the model.

**2. Making σ negative reverses the handover. Usually you can't see it, but sometimes it is as strong as the original.**
- Most negative-σ rules pack the system with relations until almost every possible one is present. The reversal is then real but vanishingly small (a few parts in a hundred thousand at most).
- In two set-ups that keep the system from filling up, the reversed handover was clearly visible:
  - with a rule against crowding, it was about as strong as typical forward handovers (index −0.112, against 0.015 to 0.19 forward);
  - with a hard rule forbidding triangles, it was weaker but plain (−0.015 to −0.042).

**3. The overall flow follows σ, even though individual loops sometimes disagree.**
- In all 36 cases with a direction (and without the special one-way behaviour of point 5), the overall direction matched the sign of σ.
- But looked at loop by loop, up to a third of the flow runs against what its own loop favours, carried along by neighbouring loops.
- So the formula explains *what pushes*; the overall pattern is a property of the whole system. I could not prove that it must always follow σ. That stays open.

**4. In ordinary (soft) rules, dissolving a relation does not enable the next step. It just clears the way.**
- Take the step "outer relation dissolves, then the source link dissolves". Removing the outer relation leaves the source link's own tendency to dissolve unchanged, or even lowers it.
- The source link's dissolution still becomes the more likely *next* event, because the outer relation's own fast dissolution is no longer competing.
- That is an **opportunity effect**, not enabling. Looking eight events ahead, the effect has almost vanished.
- Across all the soft rules, nothing was ever made possible that was impossible before. In 59% of cases, the change in "what happens next" came mainly from this opportunity effect.

**5. Real enabling needs a hard rule, and even then it need not create a direction.**
- With a rule that forbids some changes outright, dissolving a relation can make a forbidden change possible. I call this **strict enabling**. I found it in three different settings:
  - **no direction at all.** A rule forbidding triangles, or one forbidding any two relations from sharing an entity: removing one relation makes another possible in up to 87% of matched cases, yet the system has no preferred direction.
  - **a direction that follows σ.** The triangle rule plus a path rule.
  - **a new kind of direction.** A rule forbidding a relation from forming while a two-step path leads to it. Here, once a relation dissolves it cannot come back while that path exists. This **one-way release** creates the strongest flow seen in either round. It always runs "keep the better-connected link" — even when σ is negative. It is the one case where the σ rule fails.
- When something is strictly enabled, it happens before the removed relation comes back only about **half** the time. Dissolution opens a window; it does not commit the system.
- Surprisingly, the changes that dissolution makes possible are *not* more likely to come immediately afterwards. What dissolution makes possible and what tends to follow it are different questions.

**6. Two smaller boundaries.**
- **Forbidding shared entities switches off path rules completely.** Every reachable arrangement then has no two relations meeting at an entity, so a path rule never has anything to act on.
- **The fixed source can block things.** It is not just a reference point. Under some hard rules, its own internal links count against other relations forming, so no outer entity can ever link to it.

## What is a model result and what is not

- Everything above is about a small mathematical model of relations forming and dissolving.
- The direction found here is a mathematical property of chosen rules, of a kind well understood in probability theory. It is not the physical arrow of time, not thermodynamic entropy, and not gravity.
- As an interpretation for the relational framework only, the clearest lesson is that **"direction", "attraction" and "enabling" are three different things** in this model. Evidence for one says nothing about the others.
  - The handover does not pull outer entities in. Even the reversed handover leaves them less attached than with no rule at all.
  - Strict enabling can happen with no direction.

## What I recommend next (not done)

1. **Study one-way release** (my recommendation).
   - It is the only place where the σ explanation fails, and the only directed sequence without loops.
   - It is also the clearest case of a release that cannot be undone.
   - It is cheap and exact, and it bears directly on the other programme's open question about dissolution.
2. **Try to prove the overall-direction rule,** or find a counterexample (a mathematical companion to option 1).
3. **Test the fixed source's structure** (a bigger or differently shaped source). This has become more important, now that we know the source can act as a constraint, not just a reference.
4. **The "clock split" question** from E1, which E2 did not address.
5. **FREE systems with seven entities.** I'd now give this low priority: nothing found here suggests a mechanism for a centre forming by itself.

## Decisions I need from you

2. Should the two suggested findings for the **Constraint Laboratory** go to that programme? These are the exact formula for CL-Q04, and the enabling results for CL-Q05. They are written up (synthesis, section 6) but not entered in its records.

## 1. What the inquiry changed

**Before GT-P005**, the handover was E1's most robust behaviour (30 of 30 cells), but nothing explained it, and it was half-read as "dissolution enabling the next step".

**After GT-P005:**

| Level | Finding | Kind |

| Reversal | σ < 0 reverses it. Where density is held down the reversal is plainly visible: comparable to forward handovers with adjacency suppression (−0.112 against forward 0.015–0.19 at HELD N=5), weaker with hard closure exclusion (−0.015 to −0.042). It is negligible at saturation | [O] |

So the handover now has a **proven local explanation** within a stated grammar, an **empirically robust aggregate orientation** within the tested domain, and **no support** as a causal enabling mechanism in soft rules.

## 2. Findings that did not align with the expected handover

- **Reversed handovers.** These come in two sizes: negligible in saturated σ < 0 cells, and full-size where density is held down by adjacency suppression or closure exclusion.
- **One-way release.** The largest FREE irreversibility in either round (flux 0.26) has σ = 0 and orients against σ when σ < 0.
- **Enabling without direction.** The hard closure and adjacency exclusions are reversible yet strictly enabling (up to 87% of matched cases).
- **Path terms switched off by a hard adjacency exclusion.** Five rules collapse to one law.
- **The held source as a witness.** Under two hard rules, HELD collapses to a two-state chain.
- **Counter-circulation and through-flow.** These live on zero-affinity squares.
- **Precedence that misses enabling.** After an executed dissolution, the enabled formations are less likely than average as the next event.

## 3. Succession, gathering, persistence, release

- **Succession** is clearer. The model now has three distinct generators of ordered succession:
  1. soft non-gradient circulation, oriented by σ;
  2. one-way release under hard formation exclusion;
  3. none: reversible chains, even with strict enabling.

  Each is a different relation between rates, admissibility and order.
- **Gathering** was not studied directly. E2A's HELD attachment fractions are all below the null except the reversible controls, consistent with GT-F36 and GT-F18.
  - The reversed handover in ADPF did not produce gathering either: attachment 0.627 against the null 0.857.
  - Orientation of succession and attachment remain decoupled (GT-F43).
- **Persistence** is less clear than before. The race channel shows that enabled configurations persist only about as long as the support takes to return (wins about 0.5). One-way release gives a stronger kind of persistence: an *absence* that cannot be undone while supported.
- **Release.** [RS] The distinction GT-P005 asked for is now concrete. Release can be:
  - a kinetic occasion (soft);
  - an admissibility change (hard);
  - an irreversible step (one-way).

  Only the last makes release itself a directed event.

## 4. Interpretation, kept separate [RS]

- **Tendency and admissibility generate order differently.**
  - Tendency (soft weights) orders succession only through cycle affinity. The orientation is a degree comparison: relations to better-connected partners persist.
  - Admissibility (hard rules) can order succession without any cycle affinity, by making some releases unrecoverable.
  - These are two different ontological readings of "direction", and the grammar keeps them apart.
- **"Dissolution enabling a later change" has at least four non-equivalent meanings** in a relational substrate account: precedence, opportunity, rate, and support. They separate cleanly in the model, so an RS statement should name which one it means.
- **Orientation toward the better-connected partner** is a candidate motif for "relations to structure outlast relations to periphery". It is a local kinetic rule, not gathering. GT-F43's decoupling still holds.
- None of this is physics. A Markov-chain cycle arrow is not thermodynamic entropy production, and it is not an arrow of time, gravity, duration or redshift. Nothing here says what would sustain such a rule physically.

## 2. What was unexpected

- **The size of the reversed handover in ADPF.** The opposed-density cell was predeclared, but nothing predicted that reversal would be as strong as the forward handover once saturation was removed.
- **A directed mode of succession with σ = 0.** Hard path-form prohibition produces the strongest FREE irreversibility in the round, with no local cycle affinity at all. It is a distinct mechanism (one-way admissibility), not a soft cycle.
- **Enabling is invisible in precedence.** Strictly enabled events are *not* over-represented right after the enabling dissolution.
- **Strict enabling with no arrow** (EXCL). The CL-Q05 sense of "dissolution enables a distinct configuration" is fully present in a reversible chain.
- **Current through zero-affinity squares.** Its scale is large, up to 35% of flux.

## 3. How the explanation changed

| Level (GT-P005 section 3) | After E2A |
| --- | --- |
| Local rate asymmetry | The path components' cross-counts are asymmetric (far-endpoint degree); closure and adjacency are symmetric |
| Cycle affinity | Exact identity A = σ·Δdeg on adjacent squares, 0 on disjoint ones (theorem, all positive-factor rules) |
| Stationary current | Follows σ in aggregate (32/32), but not square by square (6–36% counter), with large through-flow on zero-affinity squares |
| Event-order asymmetry | Handover and partner indices take the sign of σ. At saturation they are real but negligible. The one-step release looks like enabling but is normalisation |

The handover orientation now has a **proven local explanation**, with a stated domain. Its **aggregated orientation** is an empirical regularity over the 32 cells, with no counterexample found. Its **causal reading** ("dissolution enables the next step") is **not supported** in soft rules: it is kinetic sequencing through competition for the next event.

| **Hard/soft interface: strict enabling, one-way succession and σ** | High: the only place where enabling and direction meet; the one-way mode is unexplained | High: a new mode | Is one-way succession oriented by its own rule? Does σ still predict orientation with a hard component? When does enabling bring direction? | Low (N=5) | Must not "build" an enabling example. Mitigated by a full hard × soft cross with negative controls |
| Search for aggregated-orientation counterexamples among soft rules (mixed strong/weak path pairs) | Moderate | Low | Tests the 32/32 regularity | Low | More of the same pattern |
| Precedence versus intervention, finer horizons | Moderate | Low | Measured in E2A already | Low | Low |
| Through-flow on zero-affinity squares (cycle decomposition) | Moderate | Moderate | Mathematical | Moderate (needs cycle-basis machinery) | Mostly known Markov mathematics |
| FREE N=7 hubs, source-size control, clock split (GT-Q09) | Low for this mandate; not authorised (FREE N=7) or not addressed by E2A | — | — | High | — |

**Choice: E2B maps the hard/soft interface at N=5.** The reason is that E2A revealed three relations between strict enabling and directed succession:
- enabling without direction (EXCL);
- enabling with soft direction (EXPH/EXPF);
- enabling with one-way direction (path-form prohibit, σ = 0).

The soft-rule handover itself turned out not to be enabling. The most informative next boundary is where admissibility, not rate, structures succession.

**Design principles fixed here, before writing E2B:**
- **Hard components:** the three existing hard formation exclusions — path_form prohibit, close_form prohibit and adj_form prohibit. The last is new: formation is forbidden while either endpoint has any neighbour.
- **Each crossed with soft path terms of both σ signs** (path_dissolve weak_favour, path_dissolve weak_suppress, path_form weak_suppress, path_form weak_favour), plus no soft term.
  - Combinations already run in E2A are cited, not re-run.
  - path_form soft terms are omitted under path_form prohibit, where they can never act.
- **New observables:**
  - the share of flux carried by one-way transitions;
  - one-way transitions classified by the partner-frame degree sign;
  - a race committor: after removing g, the probability that the enabled slot f toggles before g is restored.
- **Comparators and controls:**
  - the reversible hard-gradient cells (adj_form prohibit alone, close_form prohibit alone, cited from E2A);
  - the σ > 0 and σ < 0 soft partners with no hard component (cited from E2A);
  - NULL.
- **Held out for a future confirmatory test:** N=6 FREE, the strong grades, and the close_dissolve / adj hard dissolution rules (arrest-prone).
- **E2B is adaptively chosen.** It is not independent confirmation of anything in E2A.

# Release, recovery, and a reference that takes part

*A plain-English report for the human researcher on prompt GT-P006 (rounds E3A and E3B, 14 October 2026). It assumes no knowledge of the code. Detailed documents are listed at the end.*

## Where we started

In the model, entities are linked or unlinked, and links form and dissolve one at a time under local rules. The earlier rounds found two ways for such a system to run in a preferred direction:
- a gentle bias in which changes happen (a "soft" rule);
- a strict ban that stops some changes outright (a "hard" rule).

One hard rule produced **one-way release**: a link that dissolves cannot simply re-form while a two-step path leads to it. It seemed to have a direction of its own, overriding the soft rules.

You asked for two things:
- a map of what might lie between this kind of model and anything like gravity, time or motion;
- a closer look at release and recovery, keeping clear what is shown and what is not.

## What I did

1. **A map of the gap** (`docs/foundational-bridge-map.md`, written before any experiment).
   - It lists what the model can already do, what gravity-like or motion-like phenomena would need, and the links between the two.
   - Each link is labelled as proved, observed, conjectured, blocked or undefined.
   - It includes a glossary that separates words often run together: event order, clock, drift, distance, displacement, acceleration, attraction.
2. **Some mathematics** (`docs/e3-formal-support-and-recovery.md`). With the hard rule in place:
   - links can always dissolve;
   - a dissolution is one-way exactly when a two-step path leads to that link;
   - **nothing is ever lost for good**, because every arrangement can return to the empty one;
   - the shortest way back for a released link is one step more than the number of supporting links that must first dissolve.
3. **Round E3A** (27 cases plus two mathematical scans, frozen before running). It compared:
   - the hard rule with soft rules of increasing strength, using strengths the framework already has (formation slowed to 1/2, 1/4, 1/9 and 1/16, then forbidden);
   - the hard rule against opposing rules;
   - several controls, with and without a fixed source.

   It measured how released links come back: how far, how fast, and by which route.
4. **Round E3B** (18 cases, chosen *because of* what E3A showed, frozen before running). It tested whether the fixed source itself was biasing the results.

All 45 cases (27 + 18) and both scans completed. In E3A, two cases with very extreme rule strengths failed a numerical check and are flagged. A later check suggests the checking method, not the computation, was at fault (details below).

## What I found

**1. One-way release is not a separate kind of direction.**
- As formation is slowed more and more (1/2, 1/4, 1/9, 1/16), the direction, the amount of flow, and how long a released link stays away all settle at the values the hard rule gives.
- The hard ban behaves like the extreme end of an ordinary slowing rule. What is genuinely different is only the route back: a released link must wait for a supporting link to dissolve first, and can never come back directly.
- This also explains the earlier "exception": counted as an infinitely strong slowing rule, the hard ban agrees with the usual direction rule.
- The strongest opposing rule available weakened the direction a great deal (from +0.070 to +0.007) but never reversed it.

**2. Absences can persist, in two different ways.**
- A link dissolved while supported stays away longer than one dissolved unsupported.
- Under the hard rule it is **blocked** until a supporting link goes. Under soft rules it is **slow** to return, and can come back directly.
- In nearly full systems, the rare gaps that do open can last thousands of times longer than usual.

**3. The fixed source is not neutral. It quietly pushes outer entities away.**
- The fixed source is a triangle of three permanently linked entities.
- Every possible link from an outer entity to the source has exactly two supporting paths that run *inside the triangle itself*, and they are always there.
- So every rule that reads such paths applies a fixed extra factor to every attachment. For the rules that produce the handover, that factor works against attachment.
- I proved this factor cannot change any direction of flow. It only changes where the system spends its time.

**4. Removing that bias, the direction-carrying rules gather.**
- In E3B I recomputed each case with the triangle's built-in factor divided out.
- **Every rule with the usual handover direction moved from being pushed away from the source to being drawn toward it**, at both sizes tested (5 and 6 entities). Outer entities were detached about half as often. The handover kept its direction.
- One rule went from about 21 points *below* the no-rule baseline to 7 points *above* it.
- Every earlier round concluded that rules producing a direction do not gather. It now looks as if this was largely an effect of the source's shape.
- **Caveat:** the "divided-out" version is a measuring device, not a rule the model allows. A fair test needs a fixed source with no internal paths (point 6).

**5. The mathematical scan found no exception.** Over 162 combinations of rule strengths, the overall direction matched the usual rule in all 128 where it could be judged. That is evidence, not a proof.

## What has **not** been shown

- **Nothing about gravity.** No physical gravity, acceleration or time is involved.
- **"Drawn toward the source"** is a statement about how often outer entities are linked to a fixed structure in a small random model. It is not physical attraction.
- **No drift or acceleration was demonstrated.** Neither is yet defined for this model. Defining them needs an identity for "the thing that moves" and a way to measure separation that does not assume the answer.
- **The gathering result** uses a measuring device, not a rule of the model, and has not been tried at seven entities.

## What I recommend next (not done)

1. **A fixed source without internal paths** (recommended). For example, two permanently linked entities instead of three, under the same fair rules. If the direction-carrying rules gather there, the result stands without any device. This needs a small change in how the fixed source is set up, and I'd want your authorisation for it.
2. Check whether gathering-with-direction survives at **seven entities** (not authorised here).
3. Attempt a **proof of the overall-direction rule** for the smallest case.
4. Define **displacement** before any talk of motion or acceleration.

## Decisions I need from you

1. May the next prompt make the fixed source configurable (a held single edge, or other shapes), so option 1 can run?
2. Should the cross-programme notes (`docs/e3-cross-programme-transfer.md`) be passed to the Constraint Laboratory?
3. Should OP-13 to OP-15 in `docs/ontology-proposals.md` be adopted as ontology proposals? They are: "a reference takes part", "two kinds of persistence of absence", and "a hard ban as the limit of a soft one".
4. PR #6 stays a draft. Is that still right?

## Two checks I got wrong, and one flagged case

- **E3B kernel check.** In E3B, the check meant to show "nothing changed except attachments" was written badly: it divided by zero at the fixed source's own links. A direct comparison shows the identity holds exactly.
- **E3B expectation.** One E3B expectation was wrong. I said one balanced rule would be completely unchanged. Its time-weighted picture was unchanged, but its per-event picture shifted slightly.
- **E3A flagged cases.** Two extreme E3A cases failed a numerical check. The solutions themselves are accurate (residuals near 10⁻¹⁵). The checking method had not converged in one case, and its threshold was too strict in the other.

All of these are recorded as failed checks, with explanations. None of the frozen plans were changed.

## 4. Proof versus physical relevance

- **What T1–T8 are.** Statements about a declared finite stochastic grammar. They use standard Markov-chain mathematics: support graphs, communicating classes, Kolmogorov's criterion.
- **No physical arrow.** One-way release is not a physical arrow of time. Its entropy production is infinite only in the formal sense of a zero reverse rate. Nothing here models what would sustain such a rule.
- **Basin plus arrow under the instrument is a model result.** It is not attraction in any physical sense. The instrument is not a rule of the grammar.
- **Model capability is not physical mechanism.** The claim is only that, in this grammar, the reason ordered-succession rules did not gather was largely the scaffold.
- **No drift or acceleration was demonstrated.** Neither is operationally defined in this programme yet (bridge map, glossary).

## 5. Interpretation, kept separate [RS]

- **A reference is a participant, not a background.** In a relational account, whatever serves as a reference is made of relations too, and it acts on others through the same rules. The model makes this concrete: the held triangle's internal paths bias every attachment. This sits comfortably with a relational ontology that denies a neutral background. It is an interpretation, not evidence.
- **Absence can persist.** "What is not related" can be stable, either because re-formation is slow or because something must first be undone. Persistence of absence is a candidate ingredient of identity (a stable boundary), but no identity construction has been made.
- **Direction and gathering are separable but compatible.** E1 found them decoupled with the triangle scaffold. E3B shows they coexist when the scaffold's own witnesses are removed. The RS reading of GT-F43/F44 (succession and gathering are distinct notions) stands; "they cannot coexist" was never established.

# GT Round E3A — reflection and the E3A → E3B selection

*Prompt GT-P006.*
- *Written after the E3A results (result `595f4a7`, payload `1db9daa0ddff`, frozen plan `ab5f341`), and before any E3B code, plan or cell.*
- *Numbers are from `reports/round-e3a-tables.json`; every cell is in `reports/gt-e3a-atlas.md`.*
- *Layers: [O] observation, [M] mathematics, [RS] interpretation; [P] none; [T] none.*

## 1. What E3A observed

**Validation.**
- 29 of 29 analyses completed: 27 cells (8 on published kernels with new channels, 19 new) and 2 scans.
- Every identity and theorem check held: square identity I1/I2 27/27; support theorems S1 8/8; soft support S2 16/16; rate-symmetric controls S3 4/4; EXCL S4 2/2; scan diagonals S5 2/2.
- Two cells with W16 strong suppression failed the frozen numerical acceptance. They are kept and flagged *numerically qualified*:
  - **FREE N=5 PFD strong+strong (W16).** The law agrees with GTH to 2.6e-10 in L1, just over the 1e-10 tolerance; the law is exactly uniform by theorem, and the uniformity check holds at 1e-9. The fixed-point recovery reference did not converge within its cap, since recovery times reach 17,800 events.
  - **HELD N=5 PF strong (W16).** The recovery reference differs by 7e-8 on values near 270, which is 3e-10 relative, against a frozen tolerance that was absolute.
  - A **post hoc** residual check of both linear solves gives relative residuals near 1e-15 (execution record). The flags stand.

**Findings.**

1. **The hard zero continues the soft formation ladder** [O]. Along path-formation factors 1/2, 1/4, 1/9, 1/16 and 0 (FREE N=5):

   | Factor | Partner index | Flux | Witnessed releases: expected recovery time | Direct-recovery share |
   | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
   | 1/2 | 0.072 | 0.11 | 2.24 | 0.49 |
   | 1/4 | 0.104 | 0.18 | 2.82 | 0.25 |
   | 1/9 | 0.112 | 0.21 | 3.16 | 0.11 |
   | 1/16 | 0.111 | 0.22 | 3.27 | 0.06 |
   | 0 (hard) | 0.108 | 0.23 | 3.40 | 0 |

   - The orientation, flux and absence duration of the hard mode lie at the end of the soft ladder; N=4 shows the same pattern.
   - The hard mode differs **qualitatively** only in support: one-way edges, gate distance ≈ 2, and direct recovery exactly 0.
   - No limit is claimed. Positive and zero support are different kinds of chain, but the aggregate observables are continuous in practice.
2. **One-way release's orientation is the σ account with the hard component counted** [O, M sketch].
   - Hard path-form exclusion behaves as path-formation suppression with σ → +∞ on witnessed formations.
   - Adding opposing dissolution (soft σ −log 2, −log 4, −log 16) lowers the partner index from +0.070 to +0.035 to +0.007 (N=5; N=4 similar), but never reverses it.
   - This reinterprets E2B's "counterexample to σ" (GT-F51). It was a counterexample to σ computed over *soft* components only; counting the hard formation ban as unbounded positive σ restores agreement in every E2B and E3A cell.
   - This is an empirical regularity plus a heuristic reading, **not a theorem**.
3. **One-way steps and two-way circulation can pull in opposite directions** [O].
   - With the strongest opposing dissolution (W16), the part of the partner index carried by event pairs containing a one-way step is **negative**: N=4 −0.0026, N=5 −0.0006.
   - The two-way part stays positive: +0.012 and +0.0075.
   - In the plain hard cell, both parts are positive and of similar size (N=5: one-way +0.057, two-way +0.051).
   - So the aggregate can be carried by soft circulation while the hard one-way steps run against it.
4. **Absence persists longer after a witnessed release** [O].
   - In every path-suppressing cell, a relation released while path-witnessed takes longer to come back than one released unwitnessed. Hard cell, N=5: 3.40 against 2.50 time units. Soft 1/16: 3.27 against 2.43.
   - Under NULL the two are equal (1.00), so the difference is the rule, not the structure.
   - Under EXCL witnessed releases are slightly *faster* (1.72 against 1.84), because the closure exclusion acts on other relations.
5. **Two mechanisms of persistent absence** [O].
   - **Gate-limited.** In hard cells, recovery requires breaking a witness first (direct share 0; gate distance ≈ 2).
   - **Rate-limited.** In soft cells, recovery can happen directly, only slowly. The direct share falls from 0.49 to 0.06 down the ladder, so even soft recovery becomes mostly gate-clearing at strong suppression.
   - **Extreme case.** In the saturated soft σ < 0 cell (FREE N=5 PFD weak+strong), absences are rare but last very long once witnessed: 3,174 time units, against 112 unwitnessed. These are metastable holes in a nearly complete graph.
6. **The held source acts as a soft witness too** [O].
   - Under HELD N=5 path-formation suppression, a released attachment takes 18.96 time units to return at factor 1/4, and 259.77 at factor 1/16. A probe–probe relation takes about 1.
   - Recovery of attachments is 100% direct, because the source's own relations cannot be broken.
   - The numbers sit just above 4² = 16 and 16² = 256 (post hoc reading).
7. **GT-Q12 grid: no counterexample** [O]. Over 81 synthetic factor pairs at FREE N=4 (72 judged) and N=5 (56 judged; 16 below the 1e-12 floor, all at saturation), the partner index never disagreed in sign with σ. This is evidence within the grid only.

## 2. Mechanism derived after the results (labelled post hoc) [M]

Finding 6 points to a structural fact. It is derived here and has to be tested, since it was found by reading results.

- **T7 (source-witness floor).** In HELD (source {0,1,2} fixed), every attachment slot (p,s) has exactly two path witnesses lying wholly inside the source: (s, s′, s″) and (s, s″, s′). These are present in every state and never change.
  - So every path component multiplies every attachment's formation rate (path_form) or dissolution rate (path_dissolve) by a constant m².
  - Under suppression m = 1/4 that is 1/16, which matches the observed recovery near 16 + δ.
- **T8 (the floor is orientation-neutral).** A constant factor on all formations (or all dissolutions) of one slot class cancels in every cycle: in any closed cycle each slot is formed as often as it is dissolved, in both directions. So the floor changes **no cycle affinity**, and in particular not the square identity. It changes occupancy only.
  - For σ > 0 families (path_form suppress, path_dissolve favour), the floor acts **against attachment**.
  - For σ < 0 families it acts **toward** attachment.
- **Consequence (conjecture to test).** E1's observation that every arrow-carrying rule with the E0 handover orientation repels probes from the source (GT-F18) may be a **scaffold artefact**. The same σ that sets the handover direction also sets the sign of a constant source-witness bias on attachment.
  - If so, the non-gradient families' failure to gather (GT-F36, B12 on the bridge map) is at least partly produced by the held triangle's internal paths, not by the rules alone.

## 3. What changed in the explanation

| Before E3A | After E3A |
| --- | --- |
| One-way release is a distinct mechanism, unexplained, overriding σ (GT-F51, GT-Q11) | Its orientation, flux and absence durations lie at the extreme of soft formation suppression. Only support topology (one-way edges, gate ≥ 2, zero direct recovery) is qualitatively new. "Override" means the hard ban counts as unbounded σ |
| Recovery: possible (T3), kinetics unknown | Measured: witnessed releases stay absent longer. Two mechanisms, gate-limited and rate-limited; metastable holes in saturated cells |
| The held source as a hard witness (GT-F53) | Also a soft witness, with an exact constant floor (T7). That floor may explain the repulsion of every σ > 0 rule (post hoc; to test) |
| GT-Q12: 36/36 cells | Plus 128 grid points with no counterexample (still no proof) |

**Confounded or representational.**
- The partner index of hard cells mixes one-way and two-way contributions, now separated.
- Absence duration is measured in continuous time, using the cells' own rates. Comparisons across rules mix rate scale and gate structure, so the direct-recovery share is the cleaner discriminator.
- T7 is exact. Its effect on attachment margins is the open quantitative question.

**Lens A (bridge map).**
- P4 (persistent structure) gains a concrete capability: persistent absence with two distinct mechanisms. It is not persistence of an identified object.
- P1 / P8: the reference structure is not neutral, and the source-as-witness may be biasing every source–probe measurement made with path rules. **That makes the B12 → P8 "contradicted" link suspect.** It may be a scaffold result, not a result about the rules.
- P6 / P7 (displacement, acceleration): unchanged. Still not defined.

## 4. Selecting E3B

Candidates were compared factor by factor, with no combined score.

| Candidate | Information value | What it discriminates | Cost | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Source-witness neutralisation** (T7/T8): each HELD path family against its counterfactual kernel with the two wholly-internal source witnesses removed from attachment rates | **High.** It decides whether the absence of gathering in path families (GT-F18, GT-F36, B12) is a scaffold artefact. It is directly relevant to the gravity question, and tests a post hoc mechanism with a frozen prediction | Scaffold-induced repulsion against rule-intrinsic repulsion; T8 orientation-neutrality | Low (HELD N=5, 6) | The neutralised kernel is not a grammar rule (it treats source edges specially). It is an *instrument*, not a model, and must be labelled |
| Hard-ban orientation reversal search (larger N, other opposing terms) | Moderate | Whether the extended σ reading ever fails | Moderate–high (N=6 FREE) | Grid-chasing |
| Persistence-of-absence mechanisms (gate- against rate-limited, holding-time distributions) | Moderate | Already largely separated by the E3A direct-recovery share | Low | Little new |
| GT-Q12 symbolic proof at N=4 | Moderate | Proof against counterexample | Uncertain (algebra) | May not close |
| Directed displacement bridge | Low now | No non-circular displacement observable exists | — | Would be premature (bridge map) |

**Choice: E3B tests the source-witness floor.** It follows directly from what E3A revealed, and it bears most directly on the top-down question the programme started with: why the rules that order succession never gather.

**Design principles fixed here, before writing E3B:**
- **Cells.** HELD N=5 and N=6, W4 grades:
  - single path families of both σ signs (path_form weak_suppress and weak_favour; path_dissolve weak_favour and weak_suppress);
  - the E0B/E1 composites CSPH and CWPH;
  - PCOMP (σ = 0, floor on both formation and dissolution);
  - CLOSEW and NULL as controls with no path component.
- **Kernels.** Each cell is computed on its original kernel and on the **neutralised instrument kernel**: attachment rates divided by the floor factor m^(±2) per path component.
- **Frozen identities:**
  - T7: every attachment slot has exactly two wholly-internal source witnesses in every state;
  - T8: every cycle affinity is unchanged by neutralisation (square-identity residual ≤ 1e-12 against the original);
  - controls without path components are unchanged;
  - PCOMP's neutralised law equals its original law.
- **Open, no prediction.** The shift in attachment margins (four forms, both clocks); the handover index; flux; detachment. Does any σ > 0 family gather once the floor is removed?
- **E3B is adaptively chosen** and is not independent confirmation. Held out for a future test: N=7, FREE references, and other source structures.

# Does the shape of the fixed reference decide where links form?

*A plain-English report for the human researcher on prompt GT-P007 (rounds E4A and E4B, 14 October 2026). It assumes no knowledge of the code. Detailed documents are listed at the end.*

## Why this round

The last round found something awkward. The fixed reference used in every earlier experiment, a triangle of three permanently linked entities, quietly pushed outer entities away. Its own internal links count as "supporting paths" for every possible link to it, and the rules that produce a direction of flow treat supported links as harder to form or easier to break.

Dividing that effect out with a measuring device made those rules gather. But the device was not a rule the model allows, so it proved nothing on its own. You asked for a fair test: change the **shape** of the fixed reference, keep the **rules** exactly as they are, and see what happens.

## What I changed in the code

- **Any set of permanent links can now serve as the fixed reference.** Before, the triangle was hard-wired.
- **The rules still cannot tell which entities are "the source".** They read only which links are present.
- **Checks.** I confirmed that:
  - the computed rates match an independent implementation of the rules exactly, for every shape;
  - renaming the entities changes nothing except the names;
  - the triangle still reproduces every published number exactly.

## What I ran

**Round E4A** (36 cases, frozen before running). Three reference shapes, at 5 and 6 entities, under six rule sets:
- **a single link** (two entities);
- **an open path of three entities**, whose closing link is free to form and dissolve;
- **the original triangle**: these 12 cases repeat published results as a check, and all matched.

**Round E4B** (12 cases, chosen after reading E4A, frozen before running). Two four-entity shapes at 6 entities:
- **a star** (one centre linked to three others);
- **a path of four.**

All 48 cases completed, and every built-in check passed.

## What I found

**1. The reference's shape sorts where links form. This is the clearest result.**
- Within a single reference, the parts that are themselves less supported attract more links.
- In the open path, the middle entity (no permanent supporting paths) attracts about **twice** as many links as the two ends (one supporting path each).
- In the star, the centre (none) attracts about **four times** as many as the tips (two each).
- In the four-path, where every part has the same support, the difference largely disappears. One rule shows it fully; under the other two the middle still attracts a little more.
- These comparisons are made **inside the same system at the same moment**, so differences in size or crowding cannot explain them.

**2. A free link in the reference can switch a site off.** In the open path, when the closing link forms, the middle suddenly has supporting paths, and links to it drop sharply (from 41% to 14% occupancy in one rule). Under these rules the closing link itself is rarely present, because the permanent path it would close counts against it.

**3. Without permanent support at all (the single link), the direction-carrying rules do gather.**
- Under the single-link reference, every such rule gives more links to the reference than the no-rule baseline, in both ways of keeping time and at both sizes: from about 1 to 12 points above.
- This is the first time it happens with the rules unchanged.

**4. But most of that gathering comes from the system being sparse.**
- These rules keep the whole graph thin, and when few links exist, those few tend to involve the reference.
- After adjusting for how crowded the system is, most of the advantage disappears. Only one combined rule keeps a small advantage at both sizes, and it shrinks as the system grows.

**5. Total support is not what decides the overall effect.**
- The star has *more* permanent support in total than the four-path. Yet it gathers (for the simple rules) while the four-path does not.
- Having one completely unsupported site seems to matter more than the total.
- The open path is an exception: it has an unsupported middle but still sits slightly below baseline overall.

**6. The direction of flow survived every shape.** The handover kept its direction under all five references. Its strength varied, being about half as large without the triangle.

## What has **not** been shown

- **This is not attraction in any physical sense.** "Gathering" here means a fixed structure is linked more often than chance in a small random model, mostly because the model stays sparse.
- **Nothing moves.** There is still no notion of displacement, distance as a physical quantity, or acceleration.
- **The fixed reference is imposed.** It is a boundary condition, not something that formed by itself.
- **Seven or more entities were not tested** (not authorised).

## Did anything go wrong?

- **No frozen check failed in either round.**
- **One labelling fix.** The single-probe channels used a fixed entity number, which is a source entity in the four-entity shapes. Before E4B ran, I made them pick a probe whenever the usual one is part of the reference. I confirmed this changed nothing in earlier results.
- **The crowding adjustment is partly hypothetical** at 6 entities, because the systems rarely visit some of the densities it compares against. This is flagged in the tables.

## What I recommend next (not done)

1. **Derive the sorting effect mathematically** (recommended). It is robust and close enough to the rules that a proof, or at least tight bounds, should be possible.
2. **Pause to review what a "reference" should be**: imposed (as now), emergent, or none at all. Five shapes have shown that any imposed reference shapes the results through its own structure.
3. **Separate sparseness from preference** more cleanly, using the data already collected (an analysis, not a new round).
4. Test the single-link reference at **seven entities** (needs authorisation).

## Decisions I need from you

1. Should the next step be the derivation (option 1), the architecture review (option 2), or both?
2. Should the cross-programme note (`docs/e4-cross-programme-transfer.md`) go to the Constraint Laboratory?
3. Should the new ontology proposals (OP-16 and OP-17) be adopted? They are "support can make a site less available" and "gathering must survive density adjustment".
4. Should PR #6 stay a draft?

## 2. Findings by strength

**Robust (both sizes, every σ > 0 family, both clocks, covariant, within-cell controls) [O]:**
- **Attachment goes where the permanent floor is low.**
  - Within P3, the floor-0 middle attracts about twice the floor-1 ends (attachment per slot 0.29–0.37 against 0.14–0.22).
  - Within the star, the floor-0 centre attracts about four times the floor-2 leaves (0.36–0.37 against 0.085–0.093).
  - Under P4, where the floor is uniform, the orbits are level for PATHF (ends 0.146, inner 0.155). Inner vertices still attract more under PATHH (0.128 against 0.159) and CSPH (0.092 against 0.151). That is a smaller, state-dependent orbit effect with no floor difference behind it.
  - These contrasts are made inside one cell, so source size, density, probe count and the null cannot explain them.
- **A free source chord switches its endpoints' neighbour off.** When the P3 chord forms, the middle's internal witnesses rise from 0 to 2 and its attachment collapses (PATHF N=5: 0.41 to 0.14). Under σ > 0 rules the held path suppresses the chord itself (occupancy 0.23–0.29, against 0.5 under NULL).
- **The handover orientation is the same under all five references;** its magnitude varies.

**Present but qualified [O]:**
- **Native gathering in raw margins.** Under K2, every σ > 0 family is above its own null in both clocks at both sizes (+0.008 to +0.124). Under the star, PATHF and PATHH are above null (+0.032 to +0.085). This is the first label-covariant instance.
- **That gathering is mostly density composition.** Standardised against each reference's own null density profile, it is near zero or negative (K2 PATHF/PATHH: −0.030 to +0.021; star: −0.031 to −0.004), except CSPH under K2: +0.055 / +0.068 at N=5, +0.009 / +0.031 at N=6.
- **The standardised margin is partly counterfactual at N=6.** 18–31% of the null weight lies on free-edge counts of low mass (atlas overlap diagnostics).

**Negative [O]:**
- **P4 and K3 (no floor-free vertex): σ > 0 path families are below null** in raw and standardised forms (P4 PATHF −0.088, PATHH −0.077; K3 as published).
- **CSPH is below null under every four-vertex reference** (star −0.060, P4 −0.251) and under P3 at N=5 (−0.043).
- **The overall margin does not follow the total floor.** The star (total 6) gathers where P4 (total 4) does not. P3 has a floor-free site but stays slightly negative.

**Mathematics [M]:**
- **F1:** the floor formula for any held graph.
- **F2:** only K2 has zero floor everywhere.
- **F4:** per-slot constant factors are orientation-neutral (generalising T8).
- **F5:** why event-order magnitudes move without any change of affinity.

## 3. Competing explanations (GT-P007 §2)

| Possibility | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| P1 triangle-specific inhibition | **Supported for the inhibition, qualified for gathering.** Witness floors redistribute attachment and suppress it at high-floor sites, but removing them gives mainly density-composition gathering |
| P2 source size / combinatorics | **Not dominant.** Within-cell orbit contrasts are independent of size. S4 against P4 at equal k, K and r0 differ in sign |
| P3 topology beyond the floor | **Supported.** The chord's state-dependent witnesses matter (P3), and the overall margin is not a function of total floor |
| P4 clock / density artefact | **Supported for the cross-scaffold margins.** Raw gathering largely vanishes after density standardisation. Clocks agree in sign for raw margins |
| P5 structure-sensitive dynamics | **Supported.** The handover magnitude roughly halves under K2/P3 against K3; flux differs little |
| P6 no general gathering | **Partly supported.** No robust standardised gathering, except CSPH under K2 (small at N=6) |
| P7 unexpected | **Floor-guided sorting of attachment between source sites.** P3's CSPH below the triangle. A chord suppressed by the held path that witnesses it. A residual inner-vertex preference under the uniform-floor P4 (PATHH, CSPH) |

## 4. E3B, revisited

- **What survived.** The triangle's floor suppresses attachment, natively and covariantly, and the sign of the raw margins flips once no floor remains (K2).
- **What did not survive as a native result.** "These rules gather once the floor is removed" holds only in raw margins, and mostly as density composition. The E3B instrument's neutralised K3 law has larger, partly standardised-positive margins, which no native reference reproduces.
- **Mathematically still true.** T7 and T8, now generalised as F1 and F4.

## 5. Dual-lens journey

| Bottom-up capability (Lens B) | Top-down prerequisite (Lens A) |
| --- | --- |
| **Proved:** floors of any held reference (F1); K2 the only floor-free connected reference (F2); orientation-neutrality of per-slot factors (F4) | A reference's internal structure is part of the dynamics; "a source" is never neutral |
| **Observed:** attachment is sorted among source sites by floor; a free chord can switch a site off; raw gathering under floor-free references, mostly density composition | *Source–probe dependence* is now structure-dependent and mostly occupancy composition, not a robust density-independent preference |
| **Still absent:** displacement of anything identified; drift; acceleration; a non-circular separation; mutual interaction; scaling | *Identity, displacement, metric, acceleration, interaction, calibration:* **undefined.** No gravitational reading is supported |

## 6. Interpretation, kept separate [RS]

- **A reference is not a place; it is a structure, and structure sorts where relations form.** The model shows a precise version: sites of a held structure that are themselves less supported (lower witness floor) attract more new relations under rules that suppress formation along supported paths. In relational terms, support can make a site less available, not more. This is an interpretation, not a physical claim.
- **"Gathering" decomposes.** In these toy rules, apparent gathering mostly reflects where the system spends its density, not a density-independent preference. Any future gravity-motivated account built on such rules would need a mechanism that survives density standardisation.

Formal derivation of floor-guided sorting:** a closed form, or bounds, for orbit attachment as a function of floor at small N (P3, star), including the chord | High: it would turn the robust observation into a mechanism with a proof domain | Floor-driven against kinetic-competition explanations | Low | Recommended |
| B. Density-matched comparison: K2 at N against K3 at N+1 (equal probe count), analysed with occupancy/preference decomposition | Moderate: separates density composition from preference | P4-type artefacts | Low (largely existing data) | Post hoc on E4A data unless frozen |
| C. N=7 under K2/star | Moderate | Size dependence of raw gathering | Moderate | Not authorised |

| E. A displacement definition proposal | Low now | — | Low | Still premature |

**Recommendation: A, with D as a short companion.** The robust result is floor-guided sorting, and it is close enough to the grammar to admit a derivation. The weak result (raw gathering) is mostly density composition, so further gathering experiments without a new mechanism are low value. An architecture pause on references is worth taking before investing in larger scaffolds.

## 2. Mathematics added (derived after E4A, labelled) [M]

- **Floor for any connected held graph H.** The fixed floor at source vertex s equals the number of ordered held 2-paths starting at s, that is, Σ over held neighbours c of s of (deg_H(c) − 1).
  - Check: K3 gives 2 at each vertex; P3 gives endpoints 1, middle 0; K2 gives 0.
  - Proof: a witness (s, c, d) with both edges held needs (s,c) held and (c,d) held with d ∉ {s, p}, and d is never the probe p, because (c,p) is not held.
- **K2 is the only connected held reference with zero floor everywhere.**
  - Zero floor at every s needs deg_H(c) ≤ 1 for every held neighbour c of every s, so every component of H is a single edge.
  - Any connected reference with k ≥ 3 has a vertex of positive floor.
  - So one cannot remove the floor while enlarging a connected source. One can only redistribute it.
- **Corollary.** Floor heterogeneity *within* one scaffold is the natural covariant instrument (as P3 showed). Examples at k = 4: the star K1,3 has centre 0 and leaves 2; the path P4 has 1 at every vertex.

Magnitudes are smaller than E3B's neutralised K3 (for example PATHF N=6: native K2 +0.026 against neutralised K3 +0.073). The two laws were never expected to match (different k, M and witnesses) |

The E3B inference that depended on the instrument is "these rules gather once the floor is gone".
